overview: Imagine a capital where riverboats arrived with cotton, jewels and news, green-glazed bowls came from nearby kilns, and a stone inscription began with a Pali salute to the Buddha. Pegu, now Bago, led the maritime Hanthawaddy kingdom of Lower Myanmar. That kingdom grew from a southern polity founded in 1287, made Pegu its capital in the late fourteenth century, and reached a brilliant fifteenth-century peak under Queen Shin Sawbu and King Dhammaceti. The atlas starts pegu only in 1492. Takayutpi then lost the kingdom to Toungoo in 1539. Pegu remained important, but as Tabinshwehti and Bayinnaung's Toungoo capital, not as the same independent dynasty. A brief Mon-led revival ended in 1552; the First Toungoo empire collapsed in 1599, and later rulers shifted the capital north. Wet-rice fields, ports, monasteries, workshops and families continued through every royal change. The atlas keeps one Pegu shape until 1650, so this card labels each political phase instead of turning a city name into a 158-year dynasty.

periods.title: Binnya Ran II inherits a wealthy downstream kingdom
periods.summary: The atlas begins as Dhammaceti dies and Binnya Ran II succeeds. Pegu governs a commercial delta world linked to Bassein, Syriam and Martaban, while its court, ports and religious institutions remain distinct from upstream Ava.

periods.title: Takayutpi faces a rising Toungoo
periods.summary: Takayutpi inherits Hanthawaddy as Portuguese firearms and Indian Ocean connections reshape warfare. Tabinshwehti of Toungoo attacks the coast and captures Pegu in 1539, ending the old ruling line's independent kingdom.

periods.title: Pegu becomes Tabinshwehti's Toungoo capital
periods.summary: Tabinshwehti moves his capital to conquered Pegu, marries a Mon princess and adopts Mon court style. This is First Toungoo rule from Pegu, not uninterrupted Hanthawaddy independence, even when chroniclers use the capital's name.

periods.title: A short revival follows Tabinshwehti's death
periods.summary: Tabinshwehti's assassination breaks his realm apart. Smim Htaw briefly revives a Mon kingship at Pegu, but Bayinnaung recaptures the city in 1552. The independent revival is real, short and easy to lose inside a broad atlas block.

periods.title: Bayinnaung builds an imperial capital at Pegu
periods.summary: Bayinnaung reunifies Lower and Upper Myanmar, conquers far beyond them and keeps Pegu as his capital. The rebuilt Hanthawaddy city and palace belong to a vast Toungoo empire whose court included people from many conquered regions.

periods.title: Nanda struggles to hold an overextended empire
periods.summary: Nanda inherits Bayinnaung's enormous realm. Repeated campaigns, rebellion and weakening control unravel the imperial system in the 1590s; Pegu is attacked and devastated in 1599, ending its First Toungoo capital phase.

periods.title: Pegu survives after imperial collapse
periods.summary: The city and delta communities continue after 1599, but restored Toungoo power is rebuilt through other centers. Calling this an independent Pegu kingdom would confuse a surviving place, a regional name and later government with the dynasty that ended earlier.

periods.title: Ava is the royal center before the atlas seam
periods.summary: By 1635 the royal capital is at Ava. Pegu remains a Lower Myanmar city and region, yet the atlas preserves the same pegu polygon until 1650 and then replaces it broadly with ava, a cartographic seam rather than a fresh conquest that year.

sections.title: Begin by testing the atlas record

items.text: The exact indexed record is id “pegu,” label “Pegu,” circa 1492 to 1650, with “Hanthawaddy kingdom” as its imported topic. It had no card or researched override. Pagan, Burmese Kingdoms, Ava, Mon State, Arakan, Ayutthaya and Sukhothai are separate records and stay separate. A shared coastline is not an alias.

At 1492, pegu is one Polygon with one ring and 33 positions. Its bounds are 94.143° to 98.672° east and 15.678° to 18.397° north; coordinate SHA-256 is 6cf6d5a4930978806c1bfc8329fce93d9ef102d336ce3cb16c5db94cfafd5009. Tested Bago, Martaban, Thaton, Yangon, Pathein and Myaungmya fall inside. These are point tests, not a survey.

The first polygon excludes Mawlamyine, Hinthada, Pyay, Taungoo, Dawei and every tested upper center. The 1500 geometry keeps 33 positions with a tiny coordinate shift. At 1530 it expands to 49 positions, adding Mawlamyine, Hinthada and Dawei; its new SHA-256 is 2918f76493c0417dc407f007e9fdff89ca7ca746667101d12298eb5a2b450e2b. Pyay and Taungoo still test outside.

The 1530 and 1600 target coordinates are identical, even though 1530 belongs to independent Hanthawaddy and 1600 follows both the 1539 Toungoo conquest and the 1599 imperial disaster. At both dates a separate burmese-kingdoms layer owns Pyay, Taungoo, Bagan and Ava, so the atlas itself keeps parallel identities.

The id is absent at 1279, 1300 and 1400 although Hanthawaddy history begins before those later snapshots, and absent at 1650 after four atlas intervals. Point tests at 1650 put nearly every Myanmar center under ava. These polygons audit imported display coverage; they do not prove an exact ethnic or sovereign frontier.

sections.title: A southern kingdom forms, moves and negotiates

items.text: Histories commonly begin the Wareru line at Martaban in 1287 after Pagan's political collapse. Pegu became the enduring capital only later, under Binnya U in the late fourteenth century. “Hanthawaddy kingdom” therefore names a changing southern political formation, not a city that ruled unchanged from its first day.

Razadarit consolidated major Lower Myanmar centers around the end of the fourteenth century and fought long wars with Ava. Later chronicles preserve vivid campaigns, but recent scholarship warns against retelling the whole rivalry as timeless hatred between two sealed ethnic camps. Geography, revenue and rival courts mattered too.

Pegu was the downstream, commercially oriented partner in a durable upstream-downstream relationship with agrarian Ava. River rice, sea trade and access to imported goods strengthened the coast; inland grain and people still mattered. Competition and exchange could happen together, rather like two quarrelsome docks sharing one river system.

The kingdom was not one centrally measured block. Pegu, Martaban and the Irrawaddy delta had their own histories and powerful local centers. Dhammaceti's inscriptions use political language that claims a sovereign center, while modern scholarship admits uncertainty about when all southern maritime polities were truly unified under it.

Queen Shin Sawbu ruled in the mid-fifteenth century and is directly visible in a 1455 Middle Mon land dedication at Kyaikmaraw. That surviving stone is firmer evidence than later court tales: it identifies a ruling queen, a religious gift and land, while revealing little about most women's daily authority.

sections.title: Kingship, offices, war and political endings

items.text: Court rule joined a monarch, nobles, ministers, regional lords, military service and religious patronage. Wider Myanmar legal traditions allowed hierarchy and appeals to coexist, but surviving Pegu evidence favors kings, gifts and monasteries. It does not hand us a complete office chart or a village clerk's ordinary working week.

Dhammaceti had been a learned monk before succeeding Shin Sawbu. His Kalyani project used ordination rules, missions and inscriptions to strengthen both the Buddhist order and royal authority. Patronage was government as well as devotion: defining legitimate religious communities could also organize people, land and prestige around Pegu.

Early Portuguese voyages reached Pegu between 1512 and 1520, bringing merchants into a coast already tied to the Indian Ocean. Firearms and overseas specialists later helped Toungoo challenge richer Lower Myanmar. Foreign contact was neither a magic cause nor a European takeover; local rulers hired, bargained and fought for their own goals.

Tabinshwehti captured Pegu in 1539 and moved his capital there. His Mon chief queen and Mon hairstyle signaled accommodation at a mixed court. Those choices complicate a simple “Burmese conquerors versus Mon victims” picture without erasing conquest, resistance, forced service or the unequal power of a victorious dynasty.

Independent Hanthawaddy ended first in 1539, briefly revived after Tabinshwehti died in 1550, and ended again when Bayinnaung took Pegu in 1552. This card records 1552 as the final political ending. The First Toungoo capital lasted to 1599, which is a separate later phase rather than extra life for the old dynasty.

sections.title: Monsoon fields, ports and traveling goods

items.text: Lower Myanmar sits among the Irrawaddy, Sittaung and Salween estuaries, with strong monsoon rain from roughly June through October. Water enriched rice land and carried boats, yet floods, shifting channels and soggy roads made control difficult. Bassein, Syriam and Martaban connected different river mouths to maritime traffic.

Reclamation and management of monsoon water expanded Lower Myanmar's rice production over the long run. Families planted, weeded, harvested, threshed, carried and stored grain, but sources seldom name individual laborers. “Rice kingdom” means thousands of muddy tasks, not grain appearing politely at a palace door.

A 1495 to 1496 Genoese visitor called Pegu a great city and marveled at the ruler's elephants. His number of more than ten thousand elephants is an outsider's claim, not a census. The useful evidence is that foreign merchants reached the court and saw elephants as a spectacular sign of royal resources.

The first Portuguese voyages to Pegu were commercial ventures whose records attracted study for economic and financial detail. Foreign merchants saw only part of the system, but ships, brokers and ports still imply organized work by carriers, interpreters, sailors, guards, artisans and accountants long before a cargo reached the palace.

Nearby Twante kilns made green and brown glazed bowls, plates, jars, bottles, figurines and tiles. Fifteenth and sixteenth-century wares traveled as far as the Persian Gulf and Philippine shipwrecks. That reach shows technical skill and trade; a bowl found overseas does not prove Pegu's king controlled its destination.

sections.title: Monasteries, art, writing and a stone voice

items.text: Hanthawaddy rulers repaired pagodas, endowed monasteries and sponsored Buddhist texts. Such gifts supported monks and craftspeople while displaying merit and authority. Theravada Buddhism was central at court, but spirit practices and local traditions continued; a royal inscription cannot make every household believe or practice in one identical way.

Dhammaceti sent 22 senior monks and accompanying novices to Sri Lanka for renewed ordination, then established the Kalyani boundary at Pegu. The project linked Lower Myanmar to an Indian Ocean Buddhist network. It also required ships, letters, gifts, translators, ritual specialists and the king's substantial material support.

The Kalyani record originally stood on ten stones. Three carried Pali and the others communicated much of the project in Mon, with extra local detail. Damage is heavier on the Mon stones. The bilingual arrangement joined an international sacred language to a regional literary language instead of making either one everybody's speech.

Authentic opening from Dhammaceti's 1476 Kalyani inscription, shown in readable modern Myanmar-script normalization: “နမော တဿ ဘဂဝတော အရဟတော သမ္မာသမ္ဗုဒ္ဓဿ။” The carved original is Pali in fifteenth-century local letters. This modern-script display is not a tracing, photograph, facsimile of the historic letterforms or claim about ordinary conversation.

Transliteration: “Namo tassa Bhagavato arahato Sammāsambuddhassa.” Translation: “Reverence to the Blessed One, the Holy One, the Fully Enlightened One.” This is a short liturgical salutation opening a royal religious inscription. It is directly relevant to Pegu but represents formal Pali, not a reconstructed sentence spoken by market children.

sections.title: Learning, books and evidence that stays honest

items.text: The Kalyani translation says candidates first practiced writing letters and learned the refuges and precepts before novice ordination. That is concrete evidence for training within an elite monastic reform. It does not prove universal schooling, equal access for girls or a classroom in every village across Hanthawaddy.

From about 1300 to 1550, vernacular literary genres, a didactic student text and historical writing expanded. Yet manuscripts remained expensive, village monastic schooling was not extensive and widespread literacy is not demonstrated. Many children probably learned orally and practically, but no Hanthawaddy child left us a weekly lesson plan.

Pali study connected learned monks across regions, while Mon carried local inscriptions and literature. Burmese and other languages were also present in the wider political world. A port child might hear several tongues without reading any of them; multilingual streets and literacy are related possibilities, not the same skill.

Shin Sawbu's 1455 stone is the earliest securely dated Middle Mon inscription identified by its editor. It records land dedication, not a folktale or alphabet exercise. Its survival proves formal Mon writing at court and shrine while reminding us that palm-leaf notes and everyday messages were much easier to lose.

The Shwegugyi temple at Pegu used glazed plaques and Buddhist imagery, while wider Lower Myanmar art drew patrons, builders, modelers, painters and donors together. Museum objects usually preserve finished devotion better than apprentices' mistakes. We can see craft knowledge clearly, but rarely the exact age or family of each learner.

Royal families used marriage, succession and household alliances as politics. Shin Sawbu was a queen in her own right and Dhammaceti was her son-in-law and successor. These unusually visible lives show elite women could hold or transmit great authority; they do not establish how property or decisions worked in every fishing or farming home.

Society included royalty, nobles, monks, soldiers, officials, merchants, farmers, fishers, boat crews, craftspeople, servants and captives. Rank, debt, gender, war and connection to patrons changed what people could choose. Traveler descriptions favor courts and markets, so a neat ladder of classes would pretend to know more than the sources.

Most households probably combined care, food preparation, repair and income-producing work, and children likely learned by watching and helping. This is a cautious inference from labor-intensive farming, boats and workshops. Direct Hanthawaddy evidence for ordinary family size, bedtime, discipline, adoption and children's chores is too sparse for confident rules.

Fifteenth-century land gifts show that rulers and monasteries could control productive resources, while local workers made those resources useful. A donation inscription celebrates giver and shrine more readily than tenants or laborers. It cannot tell us whether one named plot was worked by relatives, hired hands, dependents or several groups.

War reshaped families through levies, flight, capture and resettlement. Bayinnaung's mixed imperial capital drew people from conquered lands, while Nanda later struggled to control manpower. Court chronicles turn movement into royal strategy; for a child, it could mean an absent parent, a new language nearby or a home left behind.

sections.title: Homes, clothes, food, work and play

items.text: Fitch distinguished an older town of light wood, cane, leaf or straw buildings from Bayinnaung's planned newer city. Brick godowns protected merchants' goods when fires raced through flammable neighborhoods. Houses varied by wealth and district, so neither a palace hall nor one traveler's warehouse describes the average family home.

Balbi entered the delta in 1583 and described pilots using the fierce rising tide from Martaban, moving “as swift as an arrow” while the flood lasted. Treat the comparison as traveler color, but take the skill seriously: crews had to read tidal timing, channels and dangerous water before any cargo reached Pegu.

Rice was the dependable staple around which fish, fruit, greens, salt, oils, sweets and imported treats could vary by season and wealth. Traveler trade lists mention rice, rice drink and sugar, but no source gives one universal Pegu menu. A palace feast and a boat crew's bowl should not be blended into dinner for everyone.

Travelers noticed wrapped cloth and light clothing suited to humid heat, while court people displayed costly textiles, jewelry and rank. Their descriptions can be curious, judgmental and selective. Cloth production, washing and mending were work; one foreign visitor's sketch cannot establish a fixed costume for every gender, age and occupation.

Twante potters built brick kilns with pointed fireboxes and column supports, stacked vessels on tubular pontils and discarded warped wasters. The kilns averaged roughly 12 by 5 meters. Clay preparation, shaping, glazing, firing and hauling required teams; an animal figurine might amuse, decorate or serve ritual, so it is not automatically a toy.

sections.title: A planned imperial city, water and public spectacle

items.text: Bayinnaung rebuilt Hanthawaddy as a fortified imperial capital, with a palace complex that archaeology and chronicles associate with numerous halls. Excavated burnt teak posts are original evidence; today's reconstructed buildings are modern interpretations. A royal compound shows concentrated power, not the floor plan of ordinary neighborhoods.

Fitch saw a square new town with walls, stone gates, watchtowers, a broad water-filled ditch and unusually straight streets shaded by palms. His famous crocodiles belong to one visitor's report. The moat and straight roads aided defense and display; they were not automatically sewers, drinking pipes or proof of perfect planning.

Archaeologists identify Hanthawaddy's city wall and several kinds of moat: water, mud and dry sections. Officials describe the water moat as defensive and a water source. That does not make untreated moat water safe, and no consulted evidence shows a household pipe network serving the whole early modern city.

The palace area remains under excavation within the ancient Mon cities proposed by Myanmar to UNESCO. Excavation can test wall lines, posts and artifacts, but the tentative-list description spans many centuries. A find from Bago must be dated before it is assigned to Shin Sawbu, Bayinnaung or an even later resident.

Royal elephants, guards, processions, gilded watchtowers and busy streets impressed foreign visitors. Such spectacle was political technology: it made hierarchy visible and organized crowds. It also consumed food, labor, timber and metal. The shiny parts survive in stories more readily than the people sweeping afterward, a useful warning about court-centered sources.

Myanmar medical traditions later organized herbal, elemental, astrological and spirit-related explanations and treatments. The official history provides broad regional background, not a fifteenth-century Pegu clinic chart. Direct evidence for Hanthawaddy physicians, midwives, healers, childbirth care, disability, injuries and ordinary access to treatment remains very sparse and uneven.

Food, boiled preparations, rest, household care and plant knowledge probably handled many ordinary illnesses, but “probably” matters. Neither trade lists of drugs nor later medical manuals identify who treated a Pegu child or which remedy worked. This card therefore names the gap instead of inventing a royal hospital or a universal herbal cure.

Fitch reports a jar of water at a religious doorway for washing feet, a practical response to bare feet, heat and dusty or muddy travel. This is direct evidence for one washing custom in a traveler's account. It is not evidence for showers, municipal tap water or equal access to plentiful clean water.

No consulted Hanthawaddy excavation or contemporary text securely identifies an ordinary household toilet, latrine design, waste pit or sewer network. The city moat was defensive waterwork, not a toilet. People certainly managed bodily waste somehow, but specifying where, who cleaned it or how safely would exceed the surviving evidence.

Conquest ended a ruling house, not the delta. After 1552 Mon communities, Buddhist institutions, ports, rice fields, kilns and family knowledge continued under Toungoo rule; after 1599 Pegu survived without being the same imperial capital. At 1650 the atlas swaps pegu for ava, but real lives did not change on one map tick.

ending.text: The independent Hanthawaddy kingdom was conquered by Tabinshwehti in 1539. A short Mon-led revival followed his death in 1550, but Bayinnaung captured Pegu in 1552, the final political ending recorded here. Pegu then flourished as the capital of a different state, the First Toungoo empire, until that system collapsed in 1599. The city, Mon communities, monasteries, rice land, ports and workshops continued after both conquests. The successor link names the atlas's separate burmese-kingdoms record for territorial rule, while the text keeps city continuity distinct from dynastic continuity and from the pegu polygon that lingers to 1650.
